title: Surface shine
hookLine: we admire gilded ceilings and neglect the soul (Letters 115)

lines: A TODDLER AND A SHINY PEBBLE.
cards: Watch a toddler on a beach. They'll pass a perfectly good sandwich to dig for one shiny pebble, then guard it like treasure. We laugh.
Letter 115 doesn't. Grown-ups do exactly the same thing, Seneca says; our pebbles are just bigger and cost more.
In his Rome, the shiny pebbles were ceilings: coffered, covered in gold leaf, over columns hauled from quarries in Egypt. People craned their necks at dinner parties to admire what was overhead.
Seneca keeps asking them to look somewhere else.

teach.b: First, the pebbles. Seneca puts it bluntly: children prize little stones and trinkets, and we prize marble and gold leaf. The only difference is that our foolishness costs more.
Second, the sight we never see.

teach.h: THE GOOD SOUL WOULD OUTSHINE IT.
teach.b: If we could look into the soul of a good person, he writes, what a beautiful sight it would be: steady, generous, unafraid, shining more than any ceiling. But it doesn't glitter on the outside, so we walk past it.

Third, the theater story. In a play by Euripides, a character delivers lines praising money as the greatest good. The audience was so offended that they rose up to drive the actor and the play off the stage.

teach.h: EURIPIDES: WAIT AND SEE HOW HE ENDS.
teach.b: Euripides himself jumped up and asked them to wait and see how the man who loved gold would end. Even that audience, Seneca says, knew the praise of gold was the villain's speech. We nod at it every day.
Fourth, polishing the inside. Seneca isn't telling anyone to tear down their kitchen. He's asking where the attention goes.
A whole afternoon choosing tiles; not one minute on a resentment that's been going for years.

teach.h: POLISH THE ROOM YOU LIVE IN.
teach.b: The ceiling gets polished, and the room you actually live in, your own mind, goes dusty.
Under the gold is where the real house is.

how: Readers of Seneca's later letters often use the gilded-ceiling image as a check: noticing how much care goes to appearances and turning some of it toward character.

o: the polish a craftsman gives fine furniture
outer glitter admired while the soul goes unseen
the glow of a person who is truly good

p: wait and see how he ends

s: Seneca tells his readers to tear down their beautiful houses
he asks where attention goes, outside or inside.
a Greek audience rose up against lines praising money as the greatest good
Euripides asked them to wait and see how the gold-lover ended.
Seneca thinks adults are wiser than children about shiny things
he says our foolishness is the same, only more expensive.

games.q: you're Euripides. the audience is on its feet, furious at your character's speech praising gold. what do you do?
o: ask them to wait and see how the man ends.
games.why: by Seneca's telling, Euripides jumped up and asked them to watch what became of the gold-lover.

practice: Think of one thing you've polished lately on the outside, a photo, a room, how you looked for an event, with no shame in it.

Then find one thing inside that's been left dusty, a grudge, an apology you owe, a fear you haven't looked at, and give it the same gentle attention, the way you'd look at a scuffed table, deciding where to start.

wordCard.voice: Surface shine. Gold on the ceiling, admired by everyone, while the soul underneath, which could shine more, goes unseen. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, 'gold': the shine Seneca keeps asking his readers to look under.

carryVoice: Your line: under the gold. A good soul would outshine any ceiling. See you tomorrow.
